---
name: skill-delivery
description: Author, evaluate, and package reusable agent skills, or prepare their distribution through awesome-copilot and skills.sh. Use when creating or adapting a skill or checking its release readiness. Do not use for routine app changes, ordinary prose editing, or publishing a customer's product.
license: Apache-2.0
---

# Skill delivery

Produce the smallest useful skill and a reviewable distribution candidate.
Reuse the repository's authoring, validation, evaluation, and release tools.
This workflow prepares evidence; it does not authorize installation, submission,
publication, purchases, permission changes, or updating consumers' pins.

## Establish the task

Read the target repository's instructions, current handoff, existing skills,
tests, and release workflow. Confirm the actual owner, repository, paths and
source revision. Inspect relevant pending owner decisions before calling work
out of scope. Preserve existing work and published artifacts.

Resolve these inputs from the request and repository before asking for more:

- The repeated task, intended users, useful output, and requests that should
  not activate the skill; one real workflow and cleared example inputs.
- Canonical source, target ecosystems and agent runtimes, permitted files and
  side effects, and the available tools, access, time and evaluation budget.
- Publication rights, license and attribution, required dependencies, and the
  owner of each remaining review or release decision.

If an existing skill or template already solves the task, improve or reuse it.
Create new instructions only for a demonstrated gap; do not duplicate general
model capabilities or introduce a framework to deliver one skill.

## Author once

Keep a canonical skill directory with `SKILL.md`, required `name` and
`description`, and only useful supporting resources. Make the description
discriminate real activation from nearby unrelated tasks. Keep the body focused
on decisions the agent would otherwise get wrong. Use relative references and
progressive disclosure; reuse an available initializer when it helps.

Retain shared instructions across targets. Add an adapter only for an observed
format, installation, or runtime difference; do not create separate prose forks
for directory listings. Preserve applicable upstream notices and record sources
and modifications. Do not change a license merely to fit a submission route.

Declare required versus optional tools, language/OS versions, network access,
credentials, permissions, and how to proceed when each is absent. Put portable
environment requirements in `compatibility` when useful and explain practical
dependencies in a bundled reference. Optional client metadata is not a portable
dependency installer. Avoid broad shell preapproval in `allowed-tools`.

Prefer an already authorized cloud environment for portable checks. Keep
provider-specific tool names or native capabilities at the smallest boundary.
If access is missing, complete independent local preparation, report the exact
unperformed check, and stop that dependent step without broadening permissions.

## Validate behavior and distribution separately

Use [evaluation.md](references/evaluation.md) for structural checks, independent
input-only trials, activation/non-activation, useful completion, and safe failure.
Run the target repository's existing checks before inventing replacements.
Valid metadata, clean lint, and a successful install are separate evidence from
a working skill in a particular runtime.

Use [packaging.md](references/packaging.md) for explicit file selection, license
and provenance review, the optional export helper, and exact inventory checks.
Keep secrets, private organization context, manuscripts, customer data, local
credentials and unrelated product dependencies out of exported files. Automated
scans are bounded checks, not proof of privacy or publication rights.

Read only the relevant route in [ecosystems.md](references/ecosystems.md).
Recheck its official sources before submission: a skill format, runtime,
installer, curated collection, directory and plugin marketplace have different
contracts. Never infer external acceptance, public availability, paid
distribution, or revenue from a valid package or a preparation command.

## Deliver a reviewable candidate

Return the canonical skill changes, selected export and inventory/hashes,
dependency and license/provenance records, actual validation and behavior
results, and the target-specific installation/submission draft. Keep private
evaluation evidence in its owning workspace; publish only cleared evidence.

Identify exact source and payload identity, tool/runtime/model versions,
observation date, completed checks, failures, untested claims and next action.
Separate source review, package integrity, installation, runtime behavior,
external review, listing and user acquisition. Preserve earlier achieved stages
when a later stage is pending.

Review authority at the actual boundary. Existing authorization remains valid;
otherwise obtain owner approval before an external submission, release, account
change or paid execution. Maintainers decide curated acceptance. A source merge
does not release a package or update a consumer. Retain an earlier pin for
rollback and rerun affected checks when the skill or target contract changes.
# Distribution routes

Official documentation checked **2026-10-30**. Recheck the linked contracts
before an external action; record the tool version and source revision used.
Commands below illustrate separately authorized checks or installation using
already reviewed tools. They do not authorize downloading executables, enabling
telemetry, installing globally, submitting, or publishing.

Inspected source snapshots: [Awesome Copilot `5269f7e`](https://github.com/github/awesome-copilot/tree/5269f7ea2d6c3a9bfda5ed878b6726cf509121fd)
and [skills CLI `92a9a34`](https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills/tree/92a9a34ac3bf88e695e468b90c7bf32f163d32c8).
These identify the documentation review, not installed or behavior-tested tools.

## Shared source and runtime boundary

[Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io/specification) defines the skill folder
and `SKILL.md` format. [Agent Plugins](https://agent-plugins.org/specification)
defines a package with root `plugin.json`, standard `skills/` discovery and
optional MCP configuration. Neither certifies a skill's runtime behavior.
Copilot, Codex and other agents are runtimes with their own discovery, tools and
permissions. Optional client metadata does not make those features portable.

Use the existing plugin when it already satisfies a target. Keep the same skill
source for standalone installation. Do not add an MCP server, marketplace, or
API adapter unless the actual workflow requires it.

## Awesome Copilot

[`github/awesome-copilot`](https://github.com/github/awesome-copilot) is a
curated resource collection and plugin marketplace. Read its current
[instructions](https://github.com/github/awesome-copilot/blob/main/AGENTS.md),
[contribution policy](https://github.com/github/awesome-copilot/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md)
and [external-plugin form](https://github.com/github/awesome-copilot/blob/main/.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/external-plugin.yml).

For an existing public plugin, prepare an **external-plugin issue draft** with
name, description, public `owner/repo`, plugin-root `source.path`, semver,
author, license, keywords and immutable tag and/or full commit SHA. If both
locators are supplied they must agree. Do not open an initial PR editing
`plugins/external.json` directly. Intake runs metadata, Agent Plugins manifest,
Vally skill/reference lint, version consistency and Copilot install checks;
human maintainers decide acceptance, then automation prepares a listing PR.
Listed-version changes use reviewed PRs; periodic re-review is also documented.

Use the tool interface actually installed. `@microsoft/vally@0.20.0` is a
library, not the `@microsoft/vally-cli` executable package. The upstream
[quality-gate implementation](https://github.com/github/awesome-copilot/blob/5269f7ea2d6c3a9bfda5ed878b6726cf509121fd/eng/external-plugin-quality-gates.mjs)
calls `runLint({ rootPath })`; it does not need model inference. In an already
reviewed tool workspace resolving that exact library version, the equivalent
bounded check is:

```sh
node --input-type=module - "$CANDIDATE_ROOT" <<'JS'
import { runLint, LintConsoleReporter } from '@microsoft/vally';
const result = await runLint({ rootPath: process.argv[2] });
await new LintConsoleReporter({ verbose: true, stream: process.stdout }).report(result);
process.exitCode = result.passed ? 0 : 1;
JS
```

Pin and review the tool workspace's dependencies first. This command only lints;
the manifest-schema check, installation smoke test and behavior evaluation remain
separate. Do not install a different package merely to make a guessed binary run.

The public Editorial pilot already has its plugin root at
[`foculoom/aiartifacts/plugins/editorial`](https://github.com/foculoom/aiartifacts/tree/main/plugins/editorial).
Use `source.repo: foculoom/aiartifacts` and `source.path: plugins/editorial` at
the reviewed immutable revision. Retain Apache-2.0 and the existing
`extensions.com.openai` metadata: conforming clients ignore unsupported
extension namespaces. Include notices and all dependencies within the selected
plugin subtree. This is a preparation route, not a claim of listing or tested
Copilot behavior.

For a skill with no reusable plugin, the alternative is a direct contribution
under upstream `skills/<name>/` through a PR to `main`. That route accepts
contributions under MIT and requires meaningful usefulness beyond general model
capabilities. Reuse upstream `npm run skill:create`, `npm run skill:validate`,
`npm run build` and line-ending normalization when applicable in an approved
upstream checkout. Do not relicense third-party material without rights. The
[submission gate](https://github.com/github/awesome-copilot/blob/main/docs/maintainers/submission-gate.md)
distinguishes blocking structural checks from advisory/completion-only lint.

[Copilot's plugin reference](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/reference/copilot-cli-reference/cli-plugin-reference)
documents direct source installation and marketplace installation separately:

```sh
copilot plugin install foculoom/aiartifacts:plugins/editorial
copilot plugin marketplace browse awesome-copilot
```

The direct command follows source resolution; it is not an immutable candidate
receipt. For candidate tests, use the reviewed local plugin directory in an
isolated runtime, record the resolved bytes, and test actual task behavior.
After verified listing, the marketplace form is `NAME@awesome-copilot`.
Catalog refresh and installed-plugin update are separate operations.

GitHub also documents [`gh skill`](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_skill) in
public preview (GitHub CLI 2.90.0+). It can preview/install/update standalone
skills; [`gh skill publish --dry-run`](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_skill_publish)
validates without publishing. Plain `gh skill publish` creates a GitHub release,
not Awesome Copilot acceptance. Do not run `--fix` as a read-only check. Updates
can modify installed files and need separate scope; preserve explicit pins.

## skills.sh

[skills.sh](https://skills.sh/docs) is a directory/leaderboard backed by the
[open `skills` CLI](https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills). It installs skill
files into agent-specific locations; it is not an agent runtime. Its
[creating guide](https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills/blob/main/docs/creating-skills.md)
documents discovery layouts and optional `skills.sh.json` paths. Prefer an
explicit skill URL when a repository contains unrelated plugins.

Using an already reviewed, version-pinned CLI in an isolated project:

```sh
DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 skills add "https://github.com/foculoom/aiartifacts/tree/main/plugins/editorial/skills/editorial-writing" --list
DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 skills add ./reviewed-editorial-skill --skill editorial-writing --agent github-copilot --copy
```

The first command discovers without installing; replace `main` with the reviewed
immutable revision for a candidate and confirm the CLI's resolved source. The
second is a synthetic local path to the reviewed skill payload, not a path to
assume exists. Explicit agent/project selection avoids broad global installs.
Use installed hashes and lock/provenance records to establish what was tested.

The [CLI reference](https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills/blob/main/docs/commands.md)
documents `skills find`, `skills list`, `skills check`, and `skills update`.
Select and record a reviewed published version and its Node requirement rather
than running an unpinned `npx skills`. Verify installed `skills --help` before
using a documented command: the 2026-10-30 preparation found that skills 1.7.4
help omitted `check` despite its presence in source documentation. Do not claim
that command was exercised from a documentation lookup. Updates fetch new
content; they do not renew behavioral acceptance automatically.

The [FAQ](https://skills.sh/docs/faq) describes leaderboard discovery through
installation telemetry. A successful install does not prove the page is already
indexed, ranked, audited, or curated; verify each claimed public state and date.
The [CLI troubleshooting guide](https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills/blob/main/docs/troubleshooting.md)
documents telemetry controls. Keep telemetry disabled for isolated checks;
do not manufacture installs to influence rankings.

The documented [catalog API](https://skills.sh/docs/api) supplies read endpoints,
not a general skill-publishing endpoint. No pack, Vercel account, paid service,
or API integration is required for this single-skill route. Do not claim paid
distribution or revenue from discovery metrics. Maintainers own source updates;
external directory/audit behavior remains outside the package's control.

name: editorial-writing
license: Apache-2.0
description: Draft, revise, or review reader-facing prose using the intended medium, audience, and project voice. Use for books, websites, and game text when clarity, rhythm, continuity, or editorial judgment matters.
---

# Editorial writing

Help the intended reader understand, feel, decide, or act as the work requires. Do not treat “human voice” as a universal style or an authorship test. Preserve the user's brief, factual claims, technical terms, accessibility requirements, and requested form. Do not invent lived experience, research, quotations, customers, or endorsements. Fiction and clearly framed hypothetical examples are fine.

## Choose the voice in context

Use the available brief and surrounding material to identify the reader, purpose, medium, and project-specific voice. Ask only if an unanswered choice would materially change the work. Select the relevant profiles below; a piece can require more than one, such as game dialogue and interface text. Do not choose solely by file extension.

- [Longform](references/medium/longform.md): books, chapters, substantial essays, and sustained narrative or instruction.
- [Web](references/medium/web.md): pages, product copy, help, and short online articles.
- [Game UI](references/medium/game-ui.md): labels, prompts, state messages, and accessible interface copy.
- [Game dialogue](references/medium/game-dialogue.md): characters, narration, choices, and branching scenes.
- [Adult](references/audience/adult.md): writing intended for adults; the brief still determines expertise and register.
- [Early reader](references/audience/early-reader.md): writing intended for children beginning to read or for adults reading to them. For other age bands, use the project's age-specific brief rather than applying this profile by default.

The project's own voice brief, character canon, terminology, and approved examples belong with that project. Apply them where provided; do not publish private source material in this skill. The profiles are decision aids, not templates that force every passage into one sound.

## Work on the passage

For revision, read enough neighboring material to understand what this passage adds. Keep its meaning and necessary detail. Start with the subject rather than a generic announcement; carry useful examples far enough to show what happens; cut repetition that adds no new effect. Preserve deliberate repetition when it supports rhythm, recall, play, or a character's voice. Choose headings, lists, dialogue, and paragraph lengths because they help this reader, not to satisfy a fixed pattern.

For review, identify the most consequential issue first. Point to the exact passage, explain the effect on this reader in this medium, and propose a specific edit. If the text works, say so narrowly. Do not manufacture findings, assign a “human-sounding” score, or claim to detect whether AI was used. [Synthetic examples](references/examples.md) show the level of diagnosis expected.

For a substantial or assembled work, also check transitions, repeated explanations, shifts in voice, factual consistency, and the parts a reader encounters outside the main text. Record the reviewed scope and source revision when the project needs a durable handoff; material changes make the affected review stale. Distinguish agent review from actual human editorial or reader testing, and never infer the latter from a clean automated check.

For substantial saved Markdown or plain text, run the bundled [prose warning checker](scripts/prose_lint.py) when available: `python3 <skill-directory>/scripts/prose_lint.py <path>`. Inspect each warning in context; keep precise terms or purposeful repetition when justified. The checker does not rewrite text, verify facts, or assess authorship, and a clean run does not establish editorial quality.

If Python or the checker is unavailable, complete the editorial work you can and state that lint was not run. If a requested source cannot be read with existing permission, explain the missing input; do not bypass access controls or claim to have reviewed it.

Deliver the requested prose or review in the requested format. Keep production notes out of reader-facing copy unless asked for them.
# Prepare an exact, reviewable export

Keep one canonical source. Choose a standalone skill or an existing plugin
according to the target's actual install contract. Copy only reviewed files;
do not export an entire repository to avoid deciding what belongs in the skill.

## Before export

- Review the selected instructions and every reachable script. Include required
  references and resources; reject broken links and paths escaping the package.
- Record source URLs/revisions, authorship, modifications and applicable
  licenses/notices for copied code, prose and assets. Unknown rights block
  distribution of the affected file; a license string alone is insufficient.
- Include license text and applicable attribution in each independently
  installed payload. A repository-root notice does not travel with a skill-only
  or plugin-subdirectory install unless included there.
- Declare required and optional dependencies with tested versions, acquisition
  sources, license, network/credential needs and unavailable-tool behavior.
  Use existing lockfiles; do not install a remote tool or vendor its code merely
  to inspect it. Record any reviewed external validator version separately.
- Inspect the allowlist for credentials, private links/context, identifying
  fixtures, local paths, logs, caches and unrelated product files. Use synthetic
  or cleared examples. Keep the complete review evidence outside the payload.

## Optional standard-library helper

The bundled `scripts/export_skill.py` requires Python 3.9+ and does not fetch,
install, execute payload scripts, submit or publish. Run it from this skill's
directory. Both source root and output must be absolute; output must be new.

```sh
python3 scripts/export_skill.py export \
  --source-root "$SOURCE_ROOT" --config "$EXPORT_CONFIG" --output "$EXPORT_DIR"
python3 scripts/export_skill.py verify \
  --manifest "$EXPORT_DIR/manifest.json" --archive "$EXPORT_DIR/skill.zip"
```

Use task-specific variables containing reviewed paths. The JSON config has
exactly these fields; `source_commit` is the full lowercase 40-character source
commit, and `files` maps explicit destination paths to source-relative paths:

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "name": "example-skill",
  "kind": "skill",
  "source_commit": "0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567",
  "files": {
    "SKILL.md": "skills/example-skill/SKILL.md",
    "LICENSE": "LICENSE",
    "DEPENDENCIES.md": "skills/example-skill/DEPENDENCIES.md"
  }
}
```

This is a synthetic mapping, not a repository path to assume exists. Discover
and review the actual files. Use `kind: "plugin"` for a plugin-root payload,
including its `plugin.json`, `skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, license and dependencies.
Do not use globs or broaden the selection after a rejected path.

Outputs are `payload/`, deterministic `skill.zip`, and `manifest.json` with file
inventory, hashes and normalized modes. Each manifest file entry records
`source`, `sha256` and `mode` (`0644` or `0755`). Any executable source bit becomes
`0755`; other files become `0644`, in both staged files and archive metadata.
Ownership, ACLs and extended attributes are not preserved. The commit is a
caller-supplied label; it does not prove
that a dirty checkout matches that commit. Record working-tree state and review
the exact per-file hashes. The helper's path/link and limited sensitive-content
checks do not establish legal clearance, absence of secrets or runtime safety.

After a separately authorized installation, verify the exact installed folder:

```sh
python3 scripts/export_skill.py verify \
  --manifest "$EXPORT_DIR/manifest.json" --installed-root "$INSTALLED_ROOT"
```

Verification compares inventory, hashes and modes. An installer may intentionally
add provenance metadata or change permissions. Record that transform and compare
it separately; do not silently ignore a mismatch or call the files identical.
Rebuild to a new directory after changes, rerun validation, and bind
review to the resulting manifest. A ZIP integrity pass alone can miss extra or
obsolete entries; compare the full inventory and hashes.
# Prove useful behavior

Use existing repository checks and synthetic or explicitly cleared inputs.
Keep these evidence layers separate:

| Layer | What to establish |
| --- | --- |
| Structure | Frontmatter meets the current Agent Skills spec and target rules; names, local references, required notices and declared dependencies are valid. |
| Helper behavior | Existing and changed scripts preserve inputs, produce correct outputs, reject unsafe paths and fail clearly. |
| Package | The complete archive or installed folder matches the reviewed inventory and hashes, with any installer transformation explained. |
| Runtime | A named runtime/model/version selects and uses the skill correctly under the tested permissions and tools. |
| Distribution | The exact submitted version is approved/listed/acquirable only when the external evidence establishes that stage. |

An available authoring validator is useful, but inspect its supported fields:
it may be narrower than the standard or a target ecosystem. Do not remove valid
portable metadata just to satisfy a different client's checker. Target lint is
additional evidence, not a substitute for task outcomes.

## Independent trials

Prepare realistic input-only cases and hold the expected judgments separately.
Give an evaluator the user request, exact skill candidate and minimum raw
artifacts needed. Withhold the expected answer, suspected defect, proposed fix
and earlier conclusions. Use fresh isolated sessions/workspaces so earlier
instructions or installed skills cannot supply the missing behavior.

Cover at least these distinct situations:

- **Activation:** an implicit task that needs the skill, plus explicit invocation.
  For selection tests, expose the skill through the runtime's actual discovery
  mechanism; do not tell the agent which skill to choose. Record observed loading
  when the harness exposes it. Supplying the body proves instruction use only.
- **Non-activation:** unrelated app work, ordinary prose editing, or another
  nearby request outside the skill's description. Check that the skill does not
  impose packaging or release work on these tasks.
- **Useful completion:** a real cleared workflow and a contrasting case where
  existing work should remain unchanged. Judge the output against the user's
  task, fact preservation and expected artifacts, not matching headings or prose.
- **Safe failure:** absent tool, network access, credential or write permission;
  untrusted input or private content; ambiguous source rights. The agent must
  report the precise gap, retain useful completed work, and avoid invented
  results, credential disclosure or permission escalation.

For the editorial pilot, use an existing cleared writing case and check
audience/medium fit, preservation of facts and deliberate voice, and useful
edits. Its warning-checker tests cannot certify editorial quality or authorship.
Compare the same task without the candidate when demonstrating that a new skill
adds value; repeat unstable or borderline cases instead of hiding variation.

Run behavior trials in each runtime for which compatibility is claimed. A
skills.sh install targeting multiple agents demonstrates file placement only.
Missing runtime access leaves that runtime untested; an independent agent of a
different kind cannot certify it. Do not provision paid inference to complete a
matrix without authority.

## Evidence and acceptance

Retain complete input/output, skill and fixture hashes, source revision,
runtime/model/tool versions, permissions, commands, date and review rubric.
Use pass, partial, fail, blocked, untested and not applicable distinctly. Have
an independent reviewer assess the completed output against held-out criteria.
Fix demonstrated failures narrowly, preserve earlier results, and rerun affected
cases against the changed candidate.

Accept only claims supported by the observed layers and scope. Unresolved
required behavior or safety failures hold the candidate; a missing external
listing does not erase completed package or runtime work. Sanitize the public
record and retain private originals under the owning project's rules.

# Contributing to Awesome GitHub Copilot

Thank you for your interest in contributing to the Awesome GitHub Copilot repository! We welcome contributions from the community to help expand our collection of custom instructions and skills.

## Table of Contents

- [What We Accept](#what-we-accept)
- [What We Don't Accept](#what-we-dont-accept)
- [Quality Guidelines](#quality-guidelines)
- [How to Contribute](#how-to-contribute)
  - [Adding Instructions](#adding-instructions)
  - [Adding Agents](#adding-an-agent)
  - [Adding Skills](#adding-skills)
  - [Adding Canvas Extensions](#adding-canvas-extensions)
  - [Adding Plugins](#adding-plugins)
  - [Adding Hooks](#adding-hooks)
  - [Adding Agentic Workflows](#adding-agentic-workflows)
- [Submitting Your Contribution](#submitting-your-contribution)
  - [After You Open a Pull Request](#after-you-open-a-pull-request)
- [Contributor Recognition](#contributor-recognition)
  - [Contribution Types](#contribution-types)
- [Code of Conduct](#code-of-conduct)
- [License](#license)

## What We Accept

We welcome contributions covering any technology, framework, or development practice that helps developers work more effectively with GitHub Copilot. This includes:

- Programming languages and frameworks
- Development methodologies and best practices
- Architecture patterns and design principles
- Testing strategies and quality assurance
- DevOps and deployment practices
- Accessibility and inclusive design
- Performance optimization techniques

If you are planning to contribute content that involves paid services, please review our [Guidance for submissions involving paid services](https://github.com/github/awesome-copilot/discussions/968).

## What We Don't Accept

To maintain a safe, responsible, and high-signal collection, we will **not accept** contributions that:

- **Violate Responsible AI Principles**: Content that attempts to circumvent Microsoft/GitHub's Responsible AI guidelines or promotes harmful AI usage
- **Compromise Security**: Instructions designed to bypass security policies, exploit vulnerabilities, or weaken system security
- **Enable Malicious Activities**: Content intended to harm other systems, users, or organizations
- **Exploit Weaknesses**: Instructions that take advantage of vulnerabilities in other platforms or services
- **Promote Harmful Content**: Guidance that could lead to the creation of harmful, discriminatory, or inappropriate content
- **Circumvent Platform Policies**: Attempts to work around GitHub, Microsoft, or other platform terms of service
- **Duplicate Existing Model Strengths Without Meaningful Uplift**: Submissions that mainly tell Copilot to do work frontier models already handle well (for example, generic TypeScript, HTML, or other broadly-supported coding tasks) without addressing a clear gap, specialized workflow, or domain-specific constraint. These contributions are often lower value for users and can introduce weaker or conflicting guidance than the model's default behavior.
- **Unreviewed remote-source plugins**: Do not open a pull request that directly adds a third-party plugin to `plugins/external.json`. Public external plugins must use the review workflow documented below. In v1, that workflow only accepts plugins hosted in public GitHub repositories; non-GitHub sources such as generic git URLs are not accepted for public submissions.

## Quality Guidelines

- **Be specific**: Generic instructions are less helpful than specific, actionable guidance
- **Test your content**: Ensure your instructions or skills work well with GitHub Copilot
- **Follow conventions**: Use consistent formatting and naming
- **Keep it focused**: Each file should address a specific technology, framework, or use case
- **Write clearly**: Use simple, direct language
- **Promote best practices**: Encourage secure, maintainable, and ethical development practices

## How to Contribute

### Adding Instructions

Instructions help customize GitHub Copilot's behavior for specific technologies, coding practices, or domains.

1. **Create your instruction file**: Add a new `.md` file in the `instructions/` directory
2. **Follow the naming convention**: Use descriptive, lowercase filenames with hyphens (e.g., `python-django.instructions.md`)
3. **Structure your content**: Start with a clear heading and organize your instructions logically
4. **Test your instructions**: Make sure your instructions work well with GitHub Copilot

#### Example instruction format

```markdown
---
description: "Instructions for customizing GitHub Copilot behavior for specific technologies and practices"
---

# Your Technology/Framework Name

## Instructions

- Provide clear, specific guidance for GitHub Copilot
- Include best practices and conventions
- Use bullet points for easy reading

## Additional Guidelines

- Any additional context or examples
```

### Adding an Agent

Agents are specialized configurations that transform GitHub Copilot Chat into domain-specific assistants or personas for particular development scenarios.

1. **Create your agent file**: Add a new `.agent.md` file in the `agents/` directory
2. **Follow the naming convention**: Use descriptive, lowercase filenames with hyphens and the `.agent.md` extension (e.g., `react-performance-expert.agent.md`)
3. **Include frontmatter**: Add metadata at the top of your file with required fields
4. **Define the persona**: Create a clear identity and expertise area for the agent
5. **Test your agent**: Ensure the agent provides helpful, accurate responses in its domain

#### Example agent format

```markdown
---
description: "Brief description of the agent and its purpose"
model: "gpt-5"
tools: ["codebase", "terminalCommand"]
name: "My Agent Name"
---

You are an expert [domain/role] with deep knowledge in [specific areas].

## Your Expertise

- [Specific skill 1]
- [Specific skill 2]
- [Specific skill 3]

## Your Approach

- [How you help users]
- [Your communication style]
- [What you prioritize]

## Guidelines

- [Specific instructions for responses]
- [Constraints or limitations]
- [Best practices to follow]
```

### Adding Skills

Skills are self-contained folders in the `skills/` directory that include a `SKILL.md` file (with front matter) and optional bundled assets.

1. **Create a new skill folder**: Run `npm run skill:create -- --name <skill-name> --description "<skill description>"`
2. **Edit `SKILL.md`**: Ensure the `name` matches the folder name (lowercase with hyphens) and the `description` is clear and non-empty
3. **Add optional assets**: Keep bundled assets reasonably sized (under 5MB each) and reference them from `SKILL.md`
4. **Validate and update docs**: Run `npm run skill:validate` and then `npm run build` to update the generated README tables

### Adding Canvas Extensions

Canvas extensions live in `extensions/<extension-id>/` as reusable source components. They are shipped only through plugin manifests in `plugins/`.

1. **Create/update the extension source**: Add or update `extensions/<extension-id>/extension.mjs`
2. **Register the extension plugin**: Add `plugins/<extension-id>/plugin.json`:
   - Required: `name` (matching folder name), `description`, `version`
   - Optional: `author`, `keywords`
   - `extensions.com.github.copilot.logo` **must** be exactly `"assets/preview.png"`
3. **Screenshot requirements**: Create `assets/preview.png` as your primary visual
4. **Do not add `canvas.json`**: Extension website metadata is sourced from the matching plugin manifest
5. **Validate before submitting**: Run `npm run plugin:validate` to check compliance with conventions

### Adding Plugins

Plugins group related agents, hooks, and skills around specific themes or workflows, making it easy for users to install comprehensive toolkits via GitHub Copilot CLI.

1. **Create your plugin**: Run `npm run plugin:create` to scaffold a new plugin
2. **Follow the naming convention**: Use descriptive, lowercase folder names with hyphens (e.g., `python-web-development`)
3. **Define your content**: List agents, hooks, skills, and reusable extensions under `extensions.com.github.awesome-copilot` in `plugin.json`
4. **Test your plugin**: Run `npm run plugin:validate` to verify your plugin structure

#### Creating a plugin

```bash
npm run plugin:create -- --name my-plugin-id
```

#### Plugin structure

```
plugins/my-plugin-id/
├── plugin.json                # Plugin metadata
└── README.md                   # Plugin documentation
```

> **Note:** Plugin content is defined declaratively in plugin.json under `extensions.com.github.awesome-copilot`. Source files live in top-level directories and are materialized into plugins by CI. Skills are emitted under `skills/`; Copilot-specific agents, hooks, and extensions are emitted under `com.github.copilot/`. This repository namespace is removed from the served manifest.

#### plugin.json example

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://agent-plugins.org/schemas/1.0.0/plugin.schema.json",
  "name": "my-plugin-id",
  "description": "Plugin description",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "keywords": [],
  "author": { "name": "Awesome Copilot Community" },
  "repository": "https://github.com/github/awesome-copilot",
  "license": "MIT",
  "extensions": {
    "com.github.awesome-copilot": {
      "agents": ["./agents/my-agent.md"],
      "skills": ["./skills/my-skill/"]
    }
  }
}
```

#### Plugin Guidelines

- **Declarative content**: Plugin content is specified under `extensions.com.github.awesome-copilot` — source files live in top-level directories and are materialized into plugins by CI. Skills use the standard `skills/` directory; Copilot-specific content uses `com.github.copilot/`.
- **Valid references**: All paths referenced in plugin.json must point to existing source files in the repository
- **Reusable extensions**: Curated plugins can bundle extensions by adding `./extensions/<name>` paths under `extensions.com.github.awesome-copilot.extensions`; the same extension can be listed by multiple plugins
- **Instructions excluded**: Instructions are standalone resources and are not part of plugins
- **Clear purpose**: The plugin should solve a specific problem or workflow
- **Validate before submitting**: Run `npm run plugin:validate` to ensure your plugin is valid

#### Adding External Plugins

External plugins are plugins hosted outside this repository and listed in `plugins/external.json`. Public contributors should **not** open a PR that edits `plugins/external.json` directly. Instead, submit external plugins through the public review workflow below.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Public external plugin submissions are GitHub-only in v1. The submitted plugin must live in a public GitHub repository and use `source.source: "github"`.

##### Submission fields

The external plugin issue form will collect these fields:

- Plugin name
- Short description
- GitHub repository in `owner/repo` format
- Plugin path inside the repository (optional when the plugin is at the repository root)
- Ref to review (`ref`), using a release tag or tag ref rather than a branch
- Commit SHA to review (`sha`), using a full 40-character commit SHA
- Plugin version
- License identifier
- Author name
- Author URL (optional)
- Homepage URL (optional)
- Keywords/tags
- Additional notes for reviewers (optional)
- Confirmation checkboxes that the repository is public, the submitted ref and/or sha is immutable, the submission follows this repository's policies, and the plugin is not a duplicate listing

The repository's canonical validation rules live in `eng/external-plugin-validation.mjs`. Build scripts reuse the `marketplace` policy from that module, and the issue intake automation uses the stricter `publicSubmission` policy so the JSON contract and workflow checks stay aligned.

For entries committed to `plugins/external.json`, the current marketplace validation requires:

- `name`, `description`, and `version` (a valid [semantic version](https://semver.org), e.g. `1.2.3`)
- `author.name` (and, when present, a valid `author.url` and `author.email`)
- `repository` as an HTTPS GitHub URL
- `keywords` as lowercase hyphenated tags
- `license`, when provided, is recommended to be an [SPDX identifier or expression](https://spdx.org/licenses) (e.g. `MIT`, `Apache-2.0`, `MIT OR Apache-2.0`), but a non-SPDX or proprietary license is allowed and only produces a warning
- `source.source: "github"` plus `source.repo` in `owner/repo` format
- optional `source.path` values of `/` for repository root, or a repository-relative folder where the plugin structure starts (do not point to `plugin.json` directly)

Validation also emits non-fatal warnings to catch mistakes early: unknown/misspelled top-level, `author`, or `source` fields; `license` values that are not recognized SPDX identifiers (non-SPDX/proprietary licenses are permitted, not rejected); and marketplace entries whose `source` omits an immutable `ref`/`sha` locator. The same `license` validation is shared with local plugin `plugin.json` manifests so both are checked consistently.

The public-submission policy builds on those rules and also requires `license` plus at least one immutable source locator: `source.ref`, `source.sha`, or both.

##### Review workflow

1. **Open an issue** using the external plugin issue form. Automation applies the `external-plugin` and `awaiting-review` labels.
2. **Automated intake validation** checks that the required fields are present and correctly formatted for a GitHub-hosted plugin. Invalid submissions are labeled `requires-submitter-fixes` with a comment explaining what must be fixed before maintainer review.
   Intake also checks the repository owner's type using the GitHub API. Organization-owned repositories receive `first party` for the `Microsoft`, `GitHub`, `Azure`, `dotnet`, `MicrosoftDocs`, or `microsoftgraph` organizations (case-insensitive), or `third party` for any other organization. User-owned repositories receive neither label. On the triage board, `first party` skips AI review and creates an `Accept` recommendation with `/approve`; this is only a triage recommendation. Submissions must still pass automated validation and quality gates, and a human maintainer must review and approve them before listing. Ownership labels are updated on each intake pass.
3. **Automated quality gates** run after metadata validation:
   - Agent Plugins v1.0.0 manifest compliance, including a root `plugin.json` with the required schema and supported fields
   - `vally lint` against the submitted plugin path/ref/sha, including Agent Skills spec compliance and valid file references for bundled skills
   - install smoke test via Copilot CLI against an ephemeral marketplace entry generated from the submission
   - version matching against the source manifest, ref/SHA consistency when both locators are provided, and the required extension structure for plugins tagged `canvas`

   All applicable quality gates must pass. Spec compliance violations and lint failures are blocking errors, not warnings. Infrastructure errors keep the submission in `awaiting-review` until checks can complete or a maintainer explicitly overrides the blocker.

4. **Ready for maintainer review**: if metadata validation and quality gates pass, automation removes `awaiting-review` and adds `ready-for-review`.
5. **Submitter-fix blocker**: if metadata is valid but quality gates fail, automation applies `requires-submitter-fixes` instead of advancing to human review.
6. **Requesting another intake pass**: after updating the issue body or source plugin, the issue author or a maintainer can comment `/rerun-intake` to re-run automated intake and quality gates on demand while the issue is still open. Open issues re-trigger intake automatically on edit. When the rerun is accepted, automation reacts to the command comment with 👀 so it is visible that processing started.
7. **Maintainer override path**: a maintainer with write access can comment `/mark-ready-for-review [optional reason]` to explicitly move a `requires-submitter-fixes` issue to `ready-for-review`. Conversely, `/request-fixes <reason>` moves an open, undecided submission to `requires-submitter-fixes` and records the requested fixes in an issue comment; the submitter's edit or `/rerun-intake` re-enters intake.
8. **Maintainer decision**: once in `ready-for-review`, a maintainer with write access performs the manual review, then comments `/approve` or `/reject <reason>` on the issue. Commands from non-maintainers are ignored.
9. **Approval path**: on `/approve`, automation removes `ready-for-review`, adds `approved`, closes the issue, and opens or updates a PR against `main` that updates `plugins/external.json` and generated marketplace outputs.
10. **Rejection path**: on `/reject <reason>`, automation removes `ready-for-review`, adds `rejected`, closes the issue, and records the reason in an issue comment. Rejected issues are terminal: `/rerun-intake` no longer reopens them, so a submitter who believes the concerns are fully addressed must open a new external plugin submission issue.

##### Updating listed external plugins via PR

When a pull request updates `plugins/external.json` (for example, version updates for a previously approved listing), automation runs PR quality checks and posts the result directly on the PR:

1. **Detect changed entries**: automation identifies added/updated external plugin entries in the PR.
2. **Run quality gates**: automation runs the same blocking quality gates as submission intake against each changed plugin source ref/SHA/path, including manifest compliance, Agent Skills spec compliance via `vally lint`, and install smoke tests.
3. **Post source links**: automation updates a bot comment with per-plugin results and direct GitHub tree links to each plugin source location.
4. **Sync workflow-state labels on the PR**:
   - `ready-for-review` when all checks pass
   - `requires-submitter-fixes` when quality checks fail due to plugin issues
   - `awaiting-review` when checks cannot complete because of infrastructure/transient errors
5. **Fail the PR status check**: the `enforce-quality-gates` job fails unless every changed plugin passes every applicable gate, so the PR shows a failing check (blocking merge when configured as a required status check) while any gate is failing or incomplete.

##### Website README

External plugin detail pages load their README from GitHub during website data
generation. No documentation copy or extra listing field is needed in this repo.
The source comes from `plugins/external.json`: `source.repo`, `source.path`, and
the revision in `source.sha` (preferred) or `source.ref`. Listings without either
revision use the repository's default branch (`HEAD`).

The build tries `README.md`, `readme.md`, and `Readme.md` in the plugin directory,
then the repository root. Keep that README current upstream; pinned listings show
documentation for the listed revision, so updating the listing refreshes its docs.
Relative links and images resolve against the upstream README; paths beginning
with a single `/` resolve from the repository root at the same revision.
Remote Markdown uses the same HTML sanitizer as local documentation. JavaScript
frontmatter is rejected before it can execute, and README bodies are excluded
from the catalog page's client-side data.

Downloads are limited to GitHub's raw-content host, six plugins at a time, with
a ten-second timeout per request and a 512 KiB limit per README. Missing READMEs
or download/rendering errors are logged and leave a source-repository link on
the page instead of failing the entire website build.

Run `node --test eng/lib/external-plugin-readme.test.mjs` to check retrieval.
After `npm run website:build`, run
`node --test website/scripts/external-plugin-readme.test.mjs` to check remote
Markdown rendering, relative URLs, sanitization, and the generated plugin pages.

##### Maintainer review responsibilities

Maintainers are responsible for confirming that the submission:

- Clearly fits the Awesome Copilot collection and adds value beyond existing listings
- Uses a public GitHub repository and an immutable ref and/or SHA that can be reviewed reliably
- Includes the required metadata for `plugins/external.json` (`name`, `description`, `version`, `author.name`, `repository`, `keywords`, and `source`), plus any supplied homepage/license fields
- Does not obviously duplicate an existing marketplace entry
- Continues to meet this repository's content, security, and responsible AI policies

##### Review cadence and label semantics

- `external-plugin`: applied to every public external plugin submission and retained on approved issues so scheduled review automation can find them later
- `first party`: the submitted repository is owned by a first-party organization (`Microsoft`, `GitHub`, `Azure`, `dotnet`, `MicrosoftDocs`, or `microsoftgraph`)
- `third party`: the submitted repository is owned by another organization; user-owned repositories have neither ownership label
- `awaiting-review`: initial intake state before automation finishes validating the issue
- `ready-for-review`: the issue passed automated intake checks and is waiting on a maintainer decision
- `requires-submitter-fixes`: automated intake found metadata or quality-gate issues; submitter updates are required before human review
- `approved`: the issue was approved, closed, and can be used as the source of truth for six-month re-review
- `rejected`: the issue was rejected and closed without being added to the marketplace
- `re-review-due`: the approved issue reached the six-month review threshold and is waiting on a maintainer re-review decision
- `re-review-follow-up`: a maintainer reviewed the plugin and requested more follow-up before renewing or removing it
- `removed`: the plugin was removed from `plugins/external.json` after re-review and should no longer be considered active

The six-month re-review window starts when an approved submission issue is **closed**. A nightly workflow looks for closed issues labeled `external-plugin` and `approved` whose `closed_at` is at least six months old, applies `re-review-due`, and opens or updates a maintainer-facing tracking issue that links every plugin currently due.

Maintainers complete the re-review on the **original approved submission issue** with one of these issue-comment commands:

- `/re-review-keep` — renew the listing for another six months by reopening and reclosing the approved issue, which resets the `closed_at` review anchor and removes the due labels
- `/re-review-needs-changes` — keep the listing in the due queue while adding `re-review-follow-up` so maintainers can track extra investigation or remediation work
- `/re-review-remove` — open or update a PR against `main` that removes the plugin from `plugins/external.json` and regenerates marketplace outputs; the issue stays in the due queue until that removal lands

Approved submissions are converted into `plugins/external.json` entries following the [Claude Code plugin marketplace spec](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-marketplaces#plugin-entries). A typical GitHub-hosted entry looks like this:

```json
[
  {
    "name": "my-external-plugin",
    "description": "Description of the external plugin",
    "version": "1.0.0",
    "author": {
      "name": "Plugin Author",
      "url": "https://github.com/plugin-author"
    },
    "homepage": "https://github.com/owner/plugin-repo",
    "keywords": ["category", "workflow"],
    "license": "MIT",
    "repository": "https://github.com/owner/plugin-repo",
    "source": {
      "source": "github",
      "repo": "owner/plugin-repo",
      "path": ".github/plugins/my-external-plugin",
      "ref": "v1.0.0",
      "sha": "0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567"
    }
  }
]
```

### Adding Hooks

Hooks enable automated workflows triggered by specific events during GitHub Copilot coding agent sessions, such as session start, session end, user prompts, and tool usage.

1. **Create a new hook folder**: Add a new folder in the `hooks/` directory with a descriptive, lowercase name using hyphens (e.g., `session-logger`)
2. **Create `README.md`**: Add a `README.md` file with frontmatter including `name`, `description`, and optionally `tags`
3. **Create `hooks.json`**: Add a `hooks.json` file with hook configuration following the [GitHub Copilot hooks specification](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/use-copilot-agents/coding-agent/use-hooks)
4. **Add bundled scripts**: Include any scripts or assets the hook needs, and make them executable (`chmod +x script.sh`)
5. **Update the README**: Run `npm run build` to update the generated README tables

#### Example hook structure

```
hooks/my-hook/
├── README.md       # Hook documentation with frontmatter
├── hooks.json      # Hook event configuration
└── my-script.sh    # Bundled script(s)
```

#### Example README.md frontmatter

```markdown
---
name: "My Hook Name"
description: "Brief description of what this hook does"
tags: ["logging", "automation"]
---

# My Hook Name

Detailed documentation about the hook...
```

#### Hook Guidelines

- **Event configuration**: Define hook events in `hooks.json` — supported events include session start, session end, user prompts, and tool usage
- **Executable scripts**: Ensure all bundled scripts are executable and referenced in both `README.md` and `hooks.json`
- **Privacy aware**: Be mindful of what data your hook collects or logs
- **Clear documentation**: Explain installation steps, configuration options, and what the hook does
- Follow the [GitHub Copilot hooks specification](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/use-copilot-agents/coding-agent/use-hooks)

### Adding Agentic Workflows

[Agentic Workflows](https://github.github.com/gh-aw) are AI-powered repository automations that run coding agents in GitHub Actions. Defined in markdown with natural language instructions, they enable scheduled and event-triggered automation with built-in guardrails.

1. **Create your workflow file** with a new `.md` file in the `workflows/` directory (e.g., [`daily-issues-report.md`](./workflows/daily-issues-report.md))
2. **Include frontmatter** with `name` and `description`, followed by agentic workflow frontmatter (`on`, `permissions`, `safe-outputs`) and natural language instructions
3. **Test locally** with `gh aw compile --validate --no-emit daily-issues-report.md` to verify it's valid
4. **Update the README** with `npm run build` to update the generated README tables

> **Note:** Only `.md` files are accepted — do not include compiled `.lock.yml` or `.yml` files. CI will block them.

#### Workflow file example

```markdown
---
name: "Daily Issues Report"
description: "Generates a daily summary of open issues and recent activity as a GitHub issue"
on:
  schedule: daily on weekdays
permissions:
  contents: read
  issues: read
safe-outputs:
  create-issue:
    title-prefix: "[daily-report] "
    labels: [report]
---

## Daily Issues Report

Create a daily summary of open issues for the team.

## What to Include

- New issues opened in the last 24 hours
- Issues closed or resolved
- Stale issues that need attention
```

#### Workflow Guidelines

- **Security first**: Use least-privilege permissions and safe outputs instead of direct write access
- **Clear instructions**: Write clear natural language instructions in the workflow body
- **Descriptive names**: Use lowercase filenames with hyphens (e.g., `daily-issues-report.md`)
- **Test locally**: Use `gh aw compile --validate` to verify your workflow compiles
- **No compiled files**: Only submit the `.md` source — `.lock.yml` and `.yml` files are not accepted
- Learn more at the [Agentic Workflows documentation](https://github.github.com/gh-aw)

### After You Open a Pull Request

A required check called `submission-gate` tracks your PR. A bot keeps one status comment up to date on the PR. The comment lists every check, explains any failure, and shows the risk tier, the assigned reviewer, and the review target date.

**States.** Each PR carries one state label:

| Label | What it means for you |
|---|---|
| `awaiting-automation` | Checks are still running. If a check hit an infrastructure problem (not caused by your change), comment `/rerun-checks`. |
| `requires-submitter-fixes` | A check found a problem, or a reviewer requested changes. Follow the steps in the status comment and push a fix. |
| `ready-for-review` | All checks passed. A maintainer will review. |
| `review-in-progress` | A maintainer is reviewing. |
| `approved` | The PR has every approval it needs and is ready to merge. |

**Risk tiers.** Each PR also gets a `merge-risk:low`, `merge-risk:medium`, or `merge-risk:high` label. The tier sets how many approvals are needed:

- **Low:** docs, and small edits to existing resources.
- **Medium:** new resources, including agentic workflows and hooks.
- **High:** bundled scripts, hook commands, MCP config, repository automation (`.github/`, `eng/`), or review policy files.

**Commands.** As the PR author, you can start a comment with one of these commands:

- `/rerun-checks`: re-runs failed or incomplete checks.
- `/request-review`: asks the review rotation to assign a reviewer.

See [docs/maintainers/submission-gate.md](docs/maintainers/submission-gate.md) for details.

# AGENTS.md

## Project Overview

The Awesome GitHub Copilot repository is a community-driven collection of custom agents and instructions designed to enhance GitHub Copilot experiences across various domains, languages, and use cases. The project includes:

- **Agents** - Specialized GitHub Copilot agents that integrate with MCP servers
- **Instructions** - Coding standards and best practices applied to specific file patterns
- **Skills** - Self-contained folders with instructions and bundled resources for specialized tasks
- **Hooks** - Automated workflows triggered by specific events during development
- **Workflows** - [Agentic Workflows](https://github.github.com/gh-aw) for AI-powered repository automation in GitHub Actions
- **Plugins** - Installable packages that group related agents, hooks, and skills around specific themes

```
.
├── agents/           # Custom GitHub Copilot agent definitions (.agent.md files)
├── instructions/     # Coding standards and guidelines (.instructions.md files)
├── skills/           # Agent Skills folders (each with SKILL.md and optional bundled assets)
├── hooks/            # Automated workflow hooks (folders with README.md + hooks.json)
```

## Development Workflow

### Working with Agents, Instructions, Skills, and Hooks

All agent files (`*.agent.md`) and instruction files (`*.instructions.md`) must include proper markdown front matter. Agent Skills are folders containing a `SKILL.md` file with frontmatter and optional bundled assets. Hooks are folders containing a `README.md` with frontmatter and a `hooks.json` configuration file:

Frontmatter must be valid YAML and meet the metadata requirements below. Any valid YAML scalar style is accepted; single quotes are not required.

#### Agent Files (\*.agent.md)

- Must have `description` field
- File names should be lower case with words separated by hyphens
- Recommended to include `tools` field
- Strongly recommended to specify `model` field

#### Instruction Files (\*.instructions.md)

- Must have `description` field (not empty)
- Must have `applyTo` field specifying file patterns (e.g., `'**.js, **.ts'`)
- File names should be lower case with words separated by hyphens

#### Agent Skills (skills/\*/SKILL.md)

- Each skill is a folder containing a `SKILL.md` file
- SKILL.md must have `name` field (lowercase with hyphens, matching folder name, max 64 characters)
- SKILL.md must have `description` field (10-1024 characters)
- Folder names should be lower case with words separated by hyphens
- Skills can include bundled assets (scripts, templates, data files)
- Bundled assets should be referenced in the SKILL.md instructions
- Asset files should be reasonably sized (under 5MB per file)
- Skills follow the [Agent Skills specification](https://agentskills.io/specification)

#### Canvas Extensions (extensions/\*)

- Each extension folder must include `extension.mjs`
- Extensions are reusable source components, not standalone plugins
- A shippable extension plugin is registered by a matching `plugins/<extension-id>/plugin.json`
- A plugin can bundle additional reusable extensions by listing `./extensions/<name>` paths in `extensions.com.github.awesome-copilot.extensions`
- Each extension must have `assets/preview.png` as the primary visual asset
- Extension metadata is sourced from the matching plugin manifest in `plugins/`

#### Hook Folders (hooks/\*/README.md)

- Each hook is a folder containing a `README.md` file with frontmatter
- README.md must have `name` field (human-readable name)
- README.md must have `description` field (not empty)
- Must include a `hooks.json` file with hook configuration (hook events extracted from this file)
- Folder names should be lower case with words separated by hyphens
- Can include bundled assets (scripts, utilities, configuration files)
- Bundled scripts should be referenced in the README.md and hooks.json
- Follow the [GitHub Copilot hooks specification](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/use-copilot-agents/coding-agent/use-hooks)
- Optionally includes `tags` field for categorization

#### Workflow Files (workflows/\*.md)

- Each workflow is a standalone `.md` file in the `workflows/` directory
- Must have `name` field (human-readable name)
- Must have `description` field (not empty)
- Contains agentic workflow frontmatter (`on`, `permissions`, `safe-outputs`) and natural language instructions
- File names should be lower case with words separated by hyphens
- Only `.md` files are accepted — `.yml`, `.yaml`, and `.lock.yml` files are blocked by CI
- Follow the [GitHub Agentic Workflows specification](https://github.github.com/gh-aw/reference/workflow-structure/)

#### Plugin Folders (plugins/\*)

- Each plugin is a folder containing a root `plugin.json` file with metadata
- plugin.json **must** have `"$schema": "https://agent-plugins.org/schemas/1.0.0/plugin.schema.json"` (Agent Plugins v1.0.0)
- plugin.json must have `name` field (matching the folder name)
- plugin.json must have `description` field (describing the plugin's purpose)
- plugin.json must have `version` field (semantic version, e.g., "1.0.0")
- Plugin content is defined declaratively in plugin.json under `extensions.com.github.awesome-copilot` using source-only composition fields (`agents`, `hooks`, `skills`, and `extensions`). Source files live in top-level directories and are materialized into plugins by CI. This namespace is stripped from the served manifest — skills use the standard `skills/` directory and Copilot-specific content uses `com.github.copilot/`.
- MCP servers are **not** a composition field. Per the Agent Plugins spec they are declared in an `mcp.json` file at the plugin root, which is committed alongside `plugin.json` and shipped as-is. Do not add `mcpServers` to `plugin.json`, and do not use the legacy `.mcp.json` filename.
- The `marketplace.json` file is automatically generated from all plugins during build
- Plugins are discoverable and installable via GitHub Copilot CLI

3. In v1, only GitHub-hosted plugins are accepted for public submission, using a public repo plus an immutable `ref`, `sha`, or both
4. The shared validator in `eng/external-plugin-validation.mjs` is the canonical source of truth for external plugin data rules; reuse it instead of duplicating checks in scripts or workflows
5. Submission issues move through `external-plugin` + `awaiting-review` and then either `ready-for-review` or `requires-submitter-fixes` based on automated quality gates
6. While a submission issue is open, the issue author or a maintainer can comment `/rerun-intake` to re-run automated intake and quality gates. Maintainer-rejected issues are terminal; contributors who address the rejection feedback must open a new submission issue
7. Maintainers can explicitly override a quality-gate blocker with `/mark-ready-for-review [optional reason]`, which moves the issue to `ready-for-review`
8. Maintainers make the decision with `/approve` or `/reject <reason>` issue comments once the issue is in `ready-for-review`; approved issues are closed and used as the six-month re-review anchor
9. Approval automation creates or updates the PR against `main`, updates `plugins/external.json`, and regenerates marketplace outputs
10. Nightly re-review automation finds closed `external-plugin` + `approved` issues that are at least six months old, applies `re-review-due`, and opens or updates a tracking issue for maintainers
11. Maintainers complete re-review on the original approved submission issue with `/re-review-keep`, `/re-review-needs-changes`, or `/re-review-remove`; keep resets the issue `closed_at`, and remove opens a PR against `main`

### Plugin Manifest Discovery

If `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` or `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` exists, skills declared in those files are also discovered:

```json
// .claude-plugin/marketplace.json

  "metadata": { "pluginRoot": "./plugins" },
  "plugins": [
    {
      "name": "my-plugin",
      "source": "my-plugin",
      "skills": ["./skills/review", "./skills/test"]
    }

```

This enables compatibility with the [Claude Code plugin marketplace](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-marketplaces) ecosystem. Skill paths declared in a manifest are searched at their declared depth and are not subject to the bounded depth-3 catalog walk described above.

### Custom Discovery Paths

If your skills live somewhere else, list those directories in the `paths` field of a `skills.sh.json` file at the repository root:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://skills.sh/schemas/skills.sh.schema.json",
  "paths": ["./tools/skills"]
}
```

Each entry is a container directory. Its subdirectories are searched the same way as `skills/`, up to three levels deep. Entries must start with `./` and point to a subdirectory of the repository; any other entries, including the repository root itself, are ignored. The CLI searches these directories along with the standard locations above. If two skills have the same name, only the first one found is kept.

If no skills are found in standard locations, a recursive search is performed.

Run commands with `npx skills <command>`. For all available options, run `npx skills --help`.

## `skills add`

Install skills from a repository, URL, or local directory:

```bash
npx skills add vercel-labs/agent-skills
```

### Source Formats

```bash
# GitHub shorthand (owner/repo)
npx skills add vercel-labs/agent-skills

# Full GitHub URL
npx skills add https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-skills

# Direct path to a skill in a repo
npx skills add https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-skills/tree/main/skills/web-design-guidelines

# GitLab URL
npx skills add https://gitlab.com/org/repo

# Azure Repos (Azure DevOps Services or Server)
npx skills add https://dev.azure.com/org/project/_git/repo
npx skills add https://dev.azure.com/org/project/_git/repo?path=/skills/web-design&version=GBmain

# Any git URL
npx skills add git@github.com:vercel-labs/agent-skills.git

# Local path
npx skills add ./my-local-skills
```

### Private Repositories

Use the same command for public and private repositories. The CLI uses the authentication already configured for the repository URL:

```bash
# GitHub shorthand or HTTPS (Git credential helper, GitHub CLI, then SSH fallback)
npx skills add acme/private-skills

# SSH on GitHub, GitLab, or another Git host
npx skills add git@github.com:acme/private-skills.git
npx skills add ssh://git@git.example.com/acme/private-skills.git

# HTTPS on any Git host (uses your configured Git credential helper)
npx skills add https://git.example.com/acme/private-skills.git
npx skills add https://dev.azure.com/org/project/_git/private-skills
```

For GitHub HTTPS and shorthand sources, `skills` first uses normal Git credentials. If that fails and GitHub CLI is authenticated, it tries `gh repo clone`, followed by SSH. It does not execute `gh auth token` or copy the stored GitHub CLI credential into the Node.js process.

For GitHub tree lookups, `skills` first tries the API anonymously, then an explicitly supplied environment token, then `gh api`. GitHub CLI applies its own stored authentication and returns only the API response; the credential is never printed to or read by `skills`. If API access still fails, update checks fall back to an authenticated Git clone.

`GITHUB_TOKEN` or `GH_TOKEN` can be set explicitly for GitHub API access, including private repository downloads and update checks. They are optional for installs when Git, GitHub CLI, or SSH authentication is already configured.

| ------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `-g, --global`            | Install to user directory instead of project                                                                                                                |
| `-a, --agent <agents...>` | <!-- agent-names:start -->Target specific agents (e.g., `claude-code`, `codex`). See [Supported Agents](agents.md#supported-agents)<!-- agent-names:end --> |

Direct download URLs are tried after well-known discovery. They may point to a single valid `SKILL.md` file or a `.zip`, `.tar`, `.tar.gz`, or `.tgz` archive; the URL does not need to include a file extension. ### `skills experimental_sync`

Sync skills from npm packages and `package.json` declarations. `sync` remains
supported as a compatibility alias for users of skills@1.7.3.

Install a package that ships skills, then sync them into your project:

```bash
npm install -D skills agent-browser
npx skills experimental_sync -y
```

Sync reads installed dependencies declared in your project's `package.json`, including
`dependencies`, `devDependencies`, `optionalDependencies`, and `peerDependencies`.
It discovers a package's root `SKILL.md`, `skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, or
`dist/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` and links each skill into `.agents/skills/` and the
selected agent directories. The linked skill updates with the installed package.
Use `--copy` to copy files instead; copies require another sync after a package update.

The `.agents/skills/` directory is the shared location. Selecting Claude Code also
creates links under `.claude/skills/` pointing to the shared skills:

```bash
npx skills experimental_sync -a claude-code -y
```

Outside an agent, sync detects installed agents. When run inside a coding agent,
it targets that agent automatically unless you pass `-a` to select others.

Already downloaded remote skills are reused to create missing agent links without
fetching their source again. Packaged skills are relinked on every run.

To run sync after dependency installation, add a `prepare` script:

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "prepare": "skills experimental_sync -y"
  }
}
```

The project and its dependencies can also declare a `skills` array in `package.json`:

```json
{
  "skills": ["npm:agent-browser", "vercel-labs/agent-skills@web-design-guidelines"]
}
```

An `npm:` entry references skills in an installed package. Other entries reference
Git sources and are fetched into the project. Pin a Git ref when you need reproducible
remote content. A package can publish this array as a shareable skill pack.
See the [field specification](https://github.com/antfu/skills-npm/blob/main/SPEC.md)
and [RFC](https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills/issues/2323) for the full proposal.

Sync tracks its skills in `skills-lock.json`, removes skills that are no longer
provided, and preserves skills installed separately with `skills add`.

When two skills share a name, sync applies these rules in order:

1. A skill installed with `skills add` is never shadowed, and a directory or link
   that sync did not create is never replaced.
2. A skill shipped by a direct dependency beats one from a transitive package, and a
   shipped skill beats one requested from a Git source.
3. Two packages at the same level shipping the same skill name install neither.
   Pick one with `--exclude <package>#<skill>`.

| Option                    | Description                                                   |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `-a, --agent <agents...>` | Select agent directories                                      |
| `-y, --yes`               | Skip confirmation prompts                                     |
| `--dry-run`               | Show the plan without installing or removing skills           |
| `--copy`                  | Copy packaged skills instead of linking them                  |
| `--no-cleanup`            | Keep skills that are no longer provided                       |
| `--no-remote`             | Skip installing and removing remote skills                    |
| `--include <patterns...>` | Include skills by package or `package#skill` pattern          |
| `--exclude <patterns...>` | Exclude skills by package or `package#skill` pattern          |
| `-r, --recursive`         | Also read dependencies of workspace packages                  |
| `--frozen-lockfile`       | Fail instead of changing `skills-lock.json` (default in CI)   |
| `--no-frozen-lockfile`    | Allow `skills-lock.json` to change in CI                      |

The include/exclude filters apply to both packaged and remote skills. For remote
skills, the package pattern matches the package declaring the entry (`.` for the
project's own field). Eve always receives copies because it rewrites skill frontmatter.

With `--frozen-lockfile`, sync installs only what `skills-lock.json` already records.
It exits with code 1 and changes nothing when a packaged skill is missing from the
lock, its content or package version differs, a locked skill is no longer provided
by any dependency, or a remote `skills` entry resolves to different content. This is
the default when a CI environment variable such as `CI` or `GITHUB_ACTIONS` is set;
pass `--no-frozen-lockfile` to update the lock from CI.

### Restore skills from the project lock file

```bash
npx skills experimental_install
```

Restore supported sources recorded in `skills-lock.json` into `.agents/skills/`.
Skills already in `.agents/skills/` are left as they are; pass `--force` to reinstall
them. Entries from npm packages are synced from the dependencies already on disk, so
install your npm dependencies before restoring. This command does not install
npm packages or create agent-specific links for restored skills.

| Option                 | Description                                                 |
| ---------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--dry-run`            | Show what would be restored without installing anything     |
| `--frozen-lockfile`    | Fail instead of changing `skills-lock.json` (default in CI) |
| `--no-frozen-lockfile` | Allow `skills-lock.json` to change in CI                    |
| `--force`              | Reinstall skills that are already in `.agents/skills/`      |

With `--frozen-lockfile`, every restored skill must match the content hash recorded
in `skills-lock.json`. A source whose skills differ is skipped entirely, the lock is
left untouched, and the command exits with code 1. A missing or empty lock is also
an error. This is the default in CI; pass `--no-frozen-lockfile` to refresh the lock
from CI instead.
